extracted.intended_audience: teachers, educators, and students of education/pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing instruction that moves learners from practical, familiar activities to more abstract, theoretical thinking; includes complementary discussion of empirical vs scientific modes of thought and the methods that cultivate scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with the concrete (make much of doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the concrete denotes thinking applied to activities for the sake of dealing effectively with present practical difficulties, 'beginning with the concrete' signifies that at the outset instruction should make much of doing—especially occupations that are not routine and require intelligent selection and adaptation of means and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical manipulations that compel thinking about meaning and relations; mere use of physical objects or sensations is not enough—if objects do not leave the mind illuminated with recognition of a meaning beyond themselves, the instruction remains as abstract as rote definitions and rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing concrete with sensibly isolated object lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: The isolated presentation of things or sensations does not by itself produce genuine concreteness or understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer continuous, purposeful occupations and activities that use materials and tools in ways that force reflection on relations, causes, and ends; object lessons that are sensibly isolated tend to be barren and dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer interest from activity to study of underlying objects and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest in successful carrying on of an activity should be gradually transferred to study of objects—their properties, consequences, structures, causes, and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities so that direct interest in outcomes creates a demand for attention to more indirect and remote matters (e.g., carpentry → geometric/mechanical problems; cooking → chemistry and physiology). This organic yield is the pedagogic 'go' from concrete to abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop delight in thinking for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: An educational outcome is an interest in intellectual matters for their own sake — a delight in thinking for the sake of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate reflective inspection and testing that become ends rather than merely means; habits of thinking generated by activities should be nurtured so they can expand into independent intellectual pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar, practically grounded starting points
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete meanings are those definitely marked off and readily apprehended, typically fixed by the demands of practical life and familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select starting examples drawn from learners' common social or practical experience (e.g., household objects, social institutions like taxes or elections) so meanings are grasped directly without laborious translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that concreteness vs abstractness is relative to the learner
rubrics_metrics.description: What is abstract at one stage of development may be concrete at another; concreteness is relative to an individual's prior acquaintance and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence instruction according to learners' current knowledge and experience; technical terms can be concrete for the expert but abstract for novices, so teaching must bridge that gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep abstract thinking as an end but not the sole end
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract thinking represents an end (thinking as its own value) but should not replace practical thinking; education should not aim to destroy ability to plan and act practically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate both practical and theoretical modes; methods that develop abstract ability at the expense of practical habit fail the educational ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure a working balance between practical and abstract thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of education should be to secure a balanced interaction of the two types of mental attitude, with regard for individual disposition so as not to hamper naturally strong powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force one pattern on all pupils; broaden narrow concrete tendencies and provide application opportunities for abstractly inclined pupils so both powers interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden concretely inclined learners by seizing opportunities within practical activities
rubrics_metrics.description: For learners with a strong concrete/executive bent, every opportunity within their practical activities should be used for developing curiosity and susceptibility to intellectual problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broadening is not violent to disposition but an expansion of it—use real-life tasks to elicit questioning and inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide application and social-relevance for abstract-inclined learners
rubrics_metrics.description: For those with a taste for abstract topics, multiply opportunities and demands for the application of ideas—translating symbolic truths into terms of social life and ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link theoretical content to social, technical, or practical problems so abstract thought is tested and enriched by application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive reliance on empirical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical thinking, which depends on past habits and repeated conjunctions of events, cannot discriminate reliably between true and false connections and is liable to several defects (post hoc fallacy, failure with the novel, laziness, and dogmatism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base instruction solely on tradition, anecdote, or habit; teach students to seek causal understanding rather than mere associative regularities and to be skeptical of 'it always happens' reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break up gross facts into minute processes (analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific method replaces crude conjunctions by breaking up coarse facts of observation into a number of minuter processes not directly accessible to perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach analytic approaches: identify independent variables, isolate elements within a phenomenon, and examine how each contributes to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary conditions one by one (experimental control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientist varies conditions one by one so as to note what happens when a given condition is eliminated or changed; observations formed by variation of conditions on the basis of theory constitute experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize controlled variation and intentional manipulation of conditions rather than passive comparison of accidental differences; where possible design tasks that vary single factors to reveal causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize active experiment over passive case comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing many accidental cases is handicapped by dependency on available diversity; active experimental method intentionally produces varied cases to test hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage learners to design and carry out experiments guided by hypotheses rather than relying solely on collecting disparate observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine analysis and synthesis (discrimination and assimilation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental thinking is a conjoint process of analysis (discrimination) and synthesis (assimilation/identification): pick out minute, significant facts and assimilate them to broader principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train learners to both dissect phenomena into measurable elements and to relate discovered elements to general facts so conclusions transfer across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute detailed measurable facts for vague, gross facts to reduce error
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing a gross multifactor notion (e.g., 'suction') by a detailed and specific fact (e.g., atmospheric pressure) increases security and certainty of inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize measurable, specific variables in explanations and instruction to make reasoning testable and less random.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote transfer by relating rare phenomena to common principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to cope with novel situations depends on assimilating exceptional cases to common, general facts (e.g., relating suction-pump behavior to the general fact of weight or pressure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to map new or rare problems onto familiar principles so they can manage novelty through transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an experimental, future-oriented mindset (produce rather than wait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific method encourages producing cases and intentionally creating conditions for inquiry rather than waiting for sufficient accidental occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster agency in inquiry: design classroom tasks where students actively create evidence and test predictions, emphasizing progress and the possibilities of deliberate manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free thought from the tyranny of sense stimuli by training abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific thought requires emancipation from the immediacy and salience of sensory stimuli, since feeble or minute elements may be more important than glaring, immediate ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop learners' power of abstraction—deliberate turning away from habitual responses to follow up less conspicuous but more significant clues; encourage attention to continuous, subtle factors as well as striking events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat experience as inclusive of reflective, experimental thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience should be vital and growing—when dominated by past habit it opposes the thoughtful, but experience that includes reflection and experiment sets us free from limiting influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame 'experience' in instruction to include reflection, controlled variation, and theory-guided observation rather than mere repetition of past cases.
